x: Ted Stimpson went off next and he ran a "blinder" and took us up into 6th place, and here again his time was faster than last year, although not approaching Pat Parker's 26.18 in 1937.
His time of 17 min. 23 secs. was only three seconds behind Pat Parker's fine run in 1938, and was the fastest of the day beating Nankeville's time by 3 seconds.

Jack Brown had put in a club record-breaking run on the final leg and his time of 17min. 15secs. beat Pat Parker's old record by 5 seconds. Jack also gained 40 seconds on the leader, and if only we had been a little closer when he took over, who could say what the result might have been.

Two new boys in our team were Pat Parker and Ted Stimpson - both destined to become Cross-country Internationals. Our winning margin on this occasion was 13 seconds only from Birchfield - a most exciting race, marred only by the death of C.

He just missed selection for the 1936 Olympic Games, and in 1937 was placed 4th with Pat Parker 3rd, Bert Footer 6th, Tom Carter 7th, Les Cohen 15th and Alf Taylor 16th in the Union Sportive C.C. race near Paris, in which Belgrave won the team race, beating all the leading French and Belgian clubs,…

Pat Parker was placed third in the 3 miles (14:28.0) and earned selection against France the following week. Don Brown was third and Percy Wright fourth in the 2 miles walk, and Eddie Pack (49.2) finished fourth in the final of the 440 yards.
Pat Parker qualified for an England vest but chose to run for Ireland. David Main has also entered the ranks of the Internationals as he also ran for Ireland.

There had been a big Open Meeting at Plymouth, and one of the chief events was a Three Miles Open in which Jim Ginty (already mentioned) and Pat Parker were second and third, the winner's time being 15m. 7.4s.

Special mention might be made of Pat Parker, who fully justified our hopes of him; Tom Carter, who, although faced with the task of tackling an opponent who was out of sight when he commenced his stage, yet reeled off mile after mile in automatic fashion.
Then Pat Parker decided that it was time the Belgrave colours were taken further forward, and he gained dozens of places, closely followed by Tom Carter.

Jim Ginty and Pat Parker were in the leading bunch, and Dan Patience and Bert Footer were close behind. The second lap showed us to have a twenty to thirty points lead over our Midland rivals but on the next lap they managed to reduce our lead slightly....

Pat Parker was placed third in the 3 miles and earned selection against France the following week. Don Brown was third and Percy Wright fourth in the 2 miles walk, and Eddie Pack finished fourth in the final of the 440 yards championship.
[illegible]h, where did the Bels come in Paris? Well Pat Parker was 3rd, Arthur Penny [illegible]th, Bert Footer 6th, Tom Carter 7th, Les Cohen 15th.

In our Jubilee year, ten years later, we gained third place in the AAA 4 x 440 yards relay, Pat Parker was 3rd in the 3 miles earning him international selection in the match against France, Don Brown was 3rd in the 2 mile walk being followed home by Percy Wright (now 93 years old and our senior member).
